label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article II, Section 2, Clause 1. The President is commander in chief of the Army and Navy and of the militia of the states when called into the actual service of the United States; he may require the written opinion of the principal officer in each executive department on any subject relating to the duties of their offices; and he has power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment.
This story is about who directs the armed forces when ships are stopped.

In Federalist 69 (March 1788) Hamilton contrasted the President, who would command the forces, with the British king, who also declares war and raises and regulates fleets and armies by his own authority.
From The Federalist No. 74 (Hamilton): “the direction of war most peculiarly demands those qualities which distinguish the exercise of power by a single hand.”
The M/V Huda stern exploded after its crew ignored repeated warnings.
The strongest argument against this is that command alone does not authorize a strike on a commercial ship and rules for vessels sit elsewhere.
We read this clause to mean the President directs the army and navy in war.
A strike on a ship after its crew ignored warnings is that direction of the forces.
Keeping direction in one commander helps the forces act as one.
